problem: Target-driven visual navigation agents trained with pixel-level features and sparse-reward DRL generalize poorly to unseen targets and scenes, learn slowly, and prior work (Zhu et al.) uses scene-specific layers, auto-terminates episodes, and ignores targets hidden in closed receptacles.
motivation: Humans navigate unseen environments using accumulated 3D spatial knowledge about object relations and by attending to a few relevant objects. Most explored trajectories fail under sparse reward but still contain useful information about intermediate places. The paper wants agents that truly understand the task (explicit stop, actionable targets) and generalize.
key_idea: Augment an LSTM A3C target-image navigation agent with a GCN-encoded 3D object adjacency knowledge graph plus attention over objects, and use hindsight-style sub-target extraction (TSE) and online imitation learning to address sparse rewards.
insight: Ablations in Table 1 show each component adds gains: IL and TSE each make plain LSTM A3C learn (which otherwise gets ~0 SR), combined IL+TSE is a bit better, KG adds a clear gain, and attention adds more, mostly on unseen scenes (static SR 32.56→41.09; actionable 17.25→21.13). Training curves show sub-targets speed convergence as a substitute for expert data. Performance still drops sharply on unseen scenes, and the graph is built from environment-provided object visibility, so the gain is partly from privileged object info.
method: Base policy: A3C with LSTM and MLP heads for π(a|s,s_g) and V, conditioned on the current observation and target image; explicit stop action, reward 10.0 on success, 0.01 terminal reward, -0.01 time penalty.
Visual features: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 features for observation and target, passed through weight-shared siamese layers and fused by an FC layer into I_t.

3D knowledge graph + GCN: nodes are the 108 AI2-THOR object types; edges connect objects both visible (within 1.5 m); object info is taken directly from AI2-THOR; one-hot node features are propagated via GCN (Kipf) to get H_t and H_g.

Attention: H_t and H_g are fused by siamese+fusion layers into Q; two FC layers and a mask of visible objects R_z give softmax weights over objects; the attended vector H_a is concatenated with visual features to produce actions, with no attention loss.

Target skill extension (TSE): from each explored trajectory, sample 5 sub-targets (observations with novel objects or other threads' targets), split the trajectory into sub-trajectories, train on all, then sync the global network to local ones.
Online imitation learning: one expert trajectory per training target, generated in reverse from the target to a random start using restricted actions and priorities, trained online early in training.
Actionable targets: targets hidden in receptacles that require the open action (with automatic close) for success.

setting.backbone: ResNet50 (ImageNet-pretrained) + siamese fusion + GCN + attention + LSTM A3C (trained from scratch, except ResNet)
setting.training_data: RL in AI2-THOR kitchens (20 train rooms) for 40M frames with 140 threads, plus one expert trajectory per training target for IL; sub-target augmentation
setting.observation: egocentric RGB target image and current view, plus object-visibility info from the simulator for graph
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: move forward/back/left/right, rotate left/right, look up/down, open, stop
setting.privileged: Ground-truth object identities and visibility (within 1.5 m) from AI2-THOR used to build the knowledge graph instead of a detector

results: The full model (KG+Attention) beats FF A3C, LSTM A3C+IL+TSE and LSTM+KG on all settings, e.g. unseen-scene static SR 41.09 vs 32.56 (LSTM+KG) and 20.97 (IL+TSE). Plain LSTM A3C and FF A3C fail to generalize. Unseen-scene SPL stays low (≤7.2), and actionable targets are much harder.
limitations: Generalization to unseen scenes and targets remains weak (low SPL), and only kitchens in AI2-THOR are evaluated.
Knowledge graph uses ground-truth object identities and visibility from the simulator and only adjacency relations, not real 3D geometry.
Baselines are limited (mainly Zhu et al.); no comparison with other modern methods; no real-robot tests.
